extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, aesthetics, literature, and humor theory; general readers interested in the theory of comedy
extracted.subtask_description: A philosophical analysis of what makes things laughable and how laughter functions socially and aesthetically. The essay identifies structural features (e.g., mechanical inelasticity, fixed grimace, imitation) and social conditions (absence of feeling, collective echo) that produce comic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic is strictly human
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic does not exist outside the pale of what is strictly HUMAN; you may laugh at an animal or object only because you detect in it some human attitude, expression, or the human caprice that shaped it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: laughing at an animal only when it has a human attitude; laughing at a hat because of the human shape or fashion behind it. This criterion locates the comic in human behavior, form or use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of feeling (emotional anesthesia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter usually accompanies an ABSENCE OF FEELING: the comic requires a soul that is calm and unruffled; emotion (pity, strong affection) defeats the laughable effect unless temporarily suspended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: to experience comic effect one must adopt a disinterested spectator stance — temporarily putting aside pity or affection. Example: you must put aside sympathy to laugh at someone who inspires pity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter requires a social echo (collective context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter appears to stand in need of an echo: it is essentially social and typically reverberates among a group; many comic effects depend on a shared social frame of reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: tales told among companions produce laughter the listener outside the group may not share; full theatres produce more uncontrolled laughter; some jokes fail in translation because they rely on group customs and ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter has a social signification / corrective function
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter functions as a SOCIAL GESTURE: by fear/derision it restrains eccentricity and inelasticity in individuals, promoting sociability and mutual adaptation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bergson treats laughter as utilitarian (a social corrective) rather than merely aesthetic: it 'softens down' mechanical inelasticity and encourages members of society to appear and act as they should.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic arises from mechanical inelasticity / automatism
rubrics_metrics.description: The laughable element often consists of a certain MECHANICAL INELASTICITY or automatism — an inability to adapt, a rigid continuation of past movements or habits where flexible adjustment is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a runner who stumbles because momentum continued; a victim of a practical joke who behaves like a machine; absent-minded persons who act according to past situations rather than present reality. This is the central thread linking many comic forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law: the more natural the cause, the more comic the effect
rubrics_metrics.description: When a comic effect can be traced back to a natural, intelligible cause (rather than appearing arbitrary), it becomes more laughable — especially when we can reconstruct the life-history of that cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a fall is more comic if we know the person fell because of a specific, natural preoccupation (e.g., Don Quixote gazing at a star) than if it were a mere accident without intelligible cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absentmindedness and systematic fixation as comic sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Absentmindedness — a mind thinking of what it has done rather than what it is doing — and its systematic, organized forms (e.g., persistent romantic obsession) are fertile sources of comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the absent-minded individual, the over-romantic who walks like a somnambulist; such traits can be exploited by comic authors because they supply coherent, cumulative mishaps that expand hilarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic vice (external, ready-made vice) vs tragic vice
rubrics_metrics.description: A vice that is comic tends to be an external, ready-made rigidity imposed on the person (a 'frame' the person steps into) rather than an internal, tragic assimilation; comic vices retain independent existence and simplify the person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for characterization: comic characters are often titled by common nouns (Le Jaloux, L'Avare) because the vice remains detachable and visible, serving as the central comic trait rather than fully integrated character psychology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic physiognomy: fixed grimace and rigidity
rubrics_metrics.description: A laughable physiognomy is one that suggests something rigid or coagulated in the normally mobile face — a unique and permanent grimace implying that the person's moral life has crystallised into a single mechanical expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish expressive beauty (stable but mobile) from comic expression (permanent stereotyped grimace). Faces that seem constantly engaged in a single action (weeping, laughing, whistling) are highly comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caricature: exaggeration to reveal latent tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: The caricaturist's art is to detect and magnify an imperceptible tendency already present in a face or form; exaggeration is a means to make visible embryonic distortions that nature suggests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For exaggeration to be comic, it must not seem arbitrary but should amplify a natural inclination (e.g., lengthening a nose in the direction nature was already inclined) so the original appears to be 'its own caricature.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic in gestures and movements: person as jointed puppet / machine
rubrics_metrics.description: Attitudes, gestures and movements are laughable in exact proportion as the body reminds us of a mere machine; a clear but subtle suggestion of a set-up mechanism inside the person produces comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artistic implication: a comic artist's originality lies in imparting a special kind of life to a puppet-like figure. Example: a public speaker whose gestures repeat mechanically, betraying automatism and provoking laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and imitation expose automatism and provoke laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Gestures that repeat or can be imitated reveal a mechanical uniformity — they cease to be fully alive and thus become laughable; imitation brings out the element of automatism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: imitation of a speaker's habitual gesture highlights its mechanical nature and is therefore intrinsically laughable. Repetition that is expected (we wait for it and it occurs) triggers laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody device: connect gestures to simple mechanical occupations
rubrics_metrics.description: Deflecting gestures (without altering form) toward a plainly mechanical occupation (sawing wood, striking an anvil, tugging a bell-rope) makes them seem intentionally mechanical and increases their comic quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use in satire/parody: suggesting a banal mechanical operation as the 'meaning' of a gesture intensifies the perception of automatism and thus the ludicrous effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tension and elasticity vs rigidity: comic as lack of elasticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Life and society require TENSION and ELASTICITY — alert attention and flexible adaptation; where these are lacking (inelasticity of body, mind or character) the result is comic rigidity that society ridicules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sociological implication: the comic marks behaviours that fail the social demand for continuous reciprocal adaptation; laughter acts to signal and correct such rigidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic effect stronger when rooted in a traceable life-history
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic incidents are intensified when the audience can trace them back to plausible origins in a person's habits, passions or systematic illusions, so the effect seems natural and coherent rather than accidental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: absentmindedness arising from an identifiable obsession (romantic reading leading to dreamlike walking) yields cumulative mishaps and larger comic expansion than isolated accidents.
